newsitem.title: ITALY: Canada asks support for Zaire humanitarian force.
newsitem.headline: Canada asks support for Zaire humanitarian force.

text.p: Canada urged countries at a World Food Summit on Wednesday to join a multinational force it has agreed to lead to help starving refugees in eastern Zaire and the United States indicated it was poised to take part.
"Hundreds of thousands of refugees are quite literally eating leaves to stay alive," Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale told the summit.
"On behalf of my prime minister, the very honourable Jean Chretien, who is responding to worldwide concern, I ask for support from all sides."

Minutes earlier, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told the summit that Washington was ready to provide humanitarian aid and suppport to refugees in Africa's Great Lakes region as soon as a mechanism could be established.

Another official, U.S. undersecretary of state for global affairs Tim Wirth, later told a news briefing that Washington intended to announce an agreement in principle to take part in the force being organised to confront the Zairean crisis.

"That is currently under very extensive discussion at the highest levels of government today and I think an announcement will shortly be made about our intention to join the international force," Wirth said.

Zaire, although not on the official agenda of the five-day summit which opened on Wednesday, has loomed large in discussion from the speaker's podium and in informal talks at the fringes of the meeting at the Rome headquarters of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali urged collective action to help "over a million starving, frightened refugees...wandering helpless in the mountains and forests of eastern Zaire".
The U.N. chief has said he expects the Security Council to give its mandate to a multinational force in a few days. He was returning to New York later on Wednesday.
"For the tribes and ethnic groups who are killing each other hunger and famine are, in the final analysis, weapons of war to be used to kill and kill again," Boutros-Ghali said.

The leader of Zaire's delegation to the summit, Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda, was reluctant to talk about the situation in his country. But he told a Reuters reporter that Boutros-Ghali's plea for action "risks coming a bit late."

Goodale said it was not Canada's intention for the multinational force to intervene in the political situation in Zaire, where ethnic Hutu refugees from previous slaughter in Rwanda and Burundi have been caught in four weeks of fighting.

"Our purpose is not to intervene or to help some settle scores with others," Goodale said. "Our purpose is solely to provide humanitarian assistance to refugees and to feed desperately hungry people."

He said Canada had offered to lead an international effort "because Canada believes that someone should step forward and take the lead now" and urged the world community to "face up to its responsibilities" by participating.
Tanzanian President Benjamin William Mkapa told Reuters in an interview that he hoped groups would stop their fighting to allow help to reach the refugees.

"My hope is that those who are combatting each other now... will respect the very noble and humanitarian mission of such a neutral force which seeks to secure the sanctuaries and the corridors," Mkapa said.
